The Chronicle of the Second Age  
They say the world was once a very different place. There were people everywhere,  
animals that were kind, and machines built for every purpose. That world is long gone  
and barely remembered. Very little information from the First Age has survived. What  
remains are remnants, scraps, and rumors.  
The First Age ended, and the Second Age began on the day the world caught ﬁre. Many  
years have passed since then. Some of the world’s scars have healed, but new  
maladies have taken their place, especially for people like me. There are countless  
beasts in the Scarred World that want to kill and eat us, and many of the worst among  
them are human. But humans are no longer alone here. The Greys arrived more than a  
millennium ago when their ship crashed, and some centuries later another vessel fell  
from the sky, carrying the creatures we now call Outsiders. Both still wait for rescues  
that do not seem to be coming. The Greys have learned to assimilate. I do not know if  
the Outsiders ever will. Humans themselves have also diverged. There are the Littles,  
whose genetics leave them far smaller than baseline humans, and the Mutants, whose  
ancestors were changed by forces they never chose.  
I have spent many years gathering the information contained in this book. My days  
traversing The Deadlands between settlements have been as rewarding as they have  
been dangerous. Within these pages are anecdotes, rumors, survival tips, warnings,  
and hard lessons, all organized to promote safer travel wherever the Scarred World  
may take you. You should skip directly to the sections most relevant to your current  
situation, but I still recommend reading beyond immediate need. Knowledge that seems  
unnecessary today has a way of becoming vital without warning.  
Within The Chronicle of the Second Age you will ﬁnd three collections of knowledge I  
have assembled. The Book of Beasts provides guidance on the creatures that roam  
The Deadlands, including many varieties of what once might have been called people. I  
hesitate to use that word. A cannibal or a raider may look human, but a person has a  
soul. At least, that is what Balangao teaches. The Book of Feats records the things  
people have learned to do in order to survive, adapt, and endure. The Book of Magic  
documents the powers that have reawakened in the Second Age, along with the gods  
tied to many of them. Not all magic is divine. Some comes from study, some from  
instinct, and some from blood. I have documented all that I have seen or been able to  
conﬁrm.  
Now that you know what this book is, I hope it helps you survive, and perhaps even  
thrive, in the Second Age. Good luck to you.

The Book of Beasts  
I did not set out to catalogue monsters. I began writing this because people kept  
dying the same ways, in the same places, for the same reasons. The Deadlands are not  
empty. They are full of things that hunt, wait, burrow, stalk, and learn. Some of them  
were shaped by radiation and time. Others are the result of magic returning without  
restraint. A few were always here, buried or dormant, and only woke once the world  
changed enough to allow it. What they all share is this: they do not care about your  
plans, your courage, or your intentions.  
This book records what I have seen, what I have survived, and what others did not. The  
creatures listed here are not here to prove anything. They exist because the world  
allows them to, and because people keep dying when they underestimate them. They  
are living parts of the Scarred World, each with habits, instincts, and patterns that  
repeat often enough to be learned. Many entries describe things that were once human,  
or still resemble us closely enough to confuse the unwary. Do not let familiarity make  
you careless. I have seen more people die because they hesitated than because they  
ran.  
Each entry includes what is known to work, what usually fails, and what signs to watch  
for before it is too late. Where exact measures and observations exist, I have recorded  
them plainly. Where knowledge is incomplete, I say so. Treat this book as a guide, not a  
promise. Nothing in The Deadlands is guaranteed. If these pages give you even a  
moment’s warning, or help you recognize danger before it closes its jaws, then they  
have done their job.  
A Note on Size  
I did not settle on these size categories to describe how tall something stands or how  
much it weighs. Those details rarely help when things go wrong. What matters is how  
much space a creature controls once it decides to move, ﬁght, or block your way.  
Some things can be slipped past. Others force you to detour, slow down, or make noise  
whether you want to or not. The larger the creature, the fewer choices you have, and  
the faster a bad situation turns fatal. Size, in this book, is about presence. It is about  
how much ground a creature dominates and how difﬁcult it is to avoid once you are  
noticed.  
These categories exist so you understand, at a glance, whether something can be  
outmaneuvered, stalled, or ignored, or whether the only real option is to leave before it  
decides where the ﬁght will happen.  
For clarity, I use the following terms throughout this book. Small creatures are easy to  
miss and easier to avoid if you stay alert. Average covers most people and animals,  
things that move and ﬁght much like we do. Massive creatures are larger than a person  
and dominate space through sheer bulk. Huge creatures are unmistakably monstrous  
and difﬁcult to confront directly. Ginormous things reshape the terrain around them

Where exact details mattered, I recorded them on a single-page record of what we  
learned through repeated encounters with each entry: how tough it is, how fast it moves,  
how it ﬁghts, and what it can endure before it ﬁnally succumbs. These records change  
as people survive longer and learn more, so I keep them separate from this book. If you  
need those details, you will ﬁnd them collected in a separate ledger alongside this  
Chronicle. What follows here is the part that does not ﬁt neatly on a page: how these  
things behave, how they hunt, and how people usually die when they assume they  
already understand them.  
I hope you ﬁnd this useful, as this information has saved my life more times that I wish  
to count.  
On Monster Senses  
Many creatures in The Deadlands do not need eyes to see. Some detect movement  
through vibration, reading the ground and structures around them as clearly as tracks in  
dust. Others follow scent, blood, or decay, picking up trails long after you believe them  
erased. Certain predators rely on acute hearing, catching breath, movement, and the  
smallest disturbances in air or structure, even in total darkness. A few perceive life itself,  
turning unerringly toward the living regardless of cover, silence, or stillness. People die  
because they assume being unseen means they are safe. In most cases, they are  
wrong.

Nilbog  
Nilbogs are small, twisted creatures with  
mocking faces and voices that never  
quite line up with their movements. They  
thrive on confusion and seem to enjoy  
being underestimated.  
Do not assume desperation makes them  
reckless. Cannibal scavengers survive  
because they know exactly how far they  
can push before a ﬁght turns against  
them.  
They dart in and out of reach, taunting  
and striking where retaliation feels clumsy  
or uncertain. Nilbogs prefer cluttered  
environments where sightlines are short  
and mistakes are easy.

ROUS  
ROUS’ are giant rodents with thick fur,

They move low to the ground and favor

Do not ignore them just because they

They gnaw through barriers that would

Scorpion, Cave  
People die to swarms because they try to  
ﬁght them one target at a time.  
Cave scorpions are heavy-bodied  
arthropods whose presence is often felt  
before it is seen, through vibration and  
shifting stone.  
Tunnel Lurker  
Tunnel lurkers are scavengers adapted to  
darkness and conﬁnement. They dress  
lightly, move quietly, and know their  
territory better than anyone passing  
through.  
They favor tunnels, caverns, and  
collapsed spaces where their reach  
matters more than speed. They strike  
when something passes too close, then  
withdraw just far enough to avoid  
retaliation.  
They wait. When they strike, it is from  
behind or below, and only long enough to  
cripple before retreating.  
Do not assume distance keeps you safe.  
Cave scorpions are built to punish  
anyone who misjudges their reach.  
If you cannot see the walls around you  
clearly, assume someone else can.

Wasp, Giant  
Giant spiders move with a patience that  
makes them easy to miss until it is too  
late. Their bodies blend into shadow and  
ruin, legs folded tight until they strike.  
Giant wasps are aggressive insects with  
bright markings and relentless focus.  
Their buzzing often comes too late to  
matter, and once they decide you’re  
worth the effort, they do not stop. They  
are, without exception, assholes.  
They favor vertical spaces, ruined  
structures, and places where prey must  
slow down. Webbing appears suddenly  
and without warning, turning movement  
into panic.  
They attack in short, violent bursts, then  
pull back just far enough to reset before  
striking again. Open ground favors them,  
and retreat only encourages pursuit.  
If you see one, you either kill it or haul  
ass out of there. If you don’t, you are  
guaranteed to see more soon.  
If the ground looks untouched, look up.

Spider swarms are made up of countless  
small bodies moving as one. They spill  
through cracks, over walls, and into  
places people forget to guard.

Serious Threats  
Ash Nomad  
When they see you, they attack. Always. If  
you hesitate because your brain is still trying  
to process what the fuck you’re looking at,  
that hesitation is usually fatal.  
Ash Nomads look like travelers until the  
riﬂes come up. They move through  
irradiated regions with a calm familiarity  
that comes from long exposure and fewer  
choices.  
Cannibal Reaver  
Cannibal Reavers are hardened veterans  
marked by intentional scars, trophies taken  
from victims, and weapons worn smooth by  
repeated use. They impose discipline on  
lesser cannibals through violence, directing  
ambushes and deciding who lives long  
enough to be useful, and who is dinner.  
They favor distance and patience,  
watching before engaging. Ash Nomads  
are rarely in a hurry, and they disengage  
the moment a ﬁght turns against them.

Grave Shepherd  
Singed Nomads survived ﬁrestorms and  
long crossings of glass-scarred ground.  
Their gear is permanently scorched and  
heat-warped, and their bodies carry  
smoke-blackened burns that never fully  
heal. Others defer to them without  
discussion, watching their movements  
and waiting for subtle cues. When a  
group moves with patience and restraint  
instead of desperation, a Singed Nomad  
is usually the reason.  
Grave Shepherds are humanoids who  
move among the dead without fear or  
hesitation. They do not ﬁght against the  
risen dead, they direct them.  
Near a Grave Shepherd the undead turn,  
advance, and strike with coordination,  
responding to gestures or quiet  
commands. Watching a living ﬁgure  
calmly control the dead is profoundly  
unsettling, and killing it is often the only  
way to make the corpses fall back into  
mindless behavior.  
Tetherling  
Tetherlings cling to ceilings and high walls  
like pale, jointless mistakes, held in place  
by sinewed anchors driven deep into  
stone or concrete. Their elongated arms  
hang limp and harmless until the moment  
they strike.  
Raider Enforcer  
Raider Enforcers wear heavier gear and  
rely on intimidation and force to break  
resistance.  
When they attack, those arms snap

ground.  
Once they commit, retreat becomes  
difﬁcult.

Zombie, Fast  
Fast zombies are clearly dead, just not  
ﬁnished yet. The skin hasn’t sloughed off,  
the eyes still focus, and the body holds  
together well enough to move the way it  
used to. They run, climb, and lunge with  
unexpected speed, mouths open awaiting  
living ﬂesh. Most people expect death to  
slow down the undead, but these haven’t  
reached that stage. Given enough time  
they'll likely decay into the shambling  
kind, but until then they are violent, direct,  
and often lethal before anyone realizes  
they picked the wrong corpse to ignore.

enough to escape or ﬁnish the job. Most  
don’t survive long, but the ones that do

Light Consumer  
Some people say Light Consumers don’t  
really exist, that they’re just a story told to  
scare travelers into keeping watch. The  
stories all sound the same though. Lights that  
dim for no reason. Flames that pull inward  
instead of going out. Shadows that feel  
heavier once the glow is gone. No one  
agrees on what happens next, only that  
people disappear after the dark settles in.  
Maybe it’s coincidence. Maybe it’s something  
listening when the ﬁre burns too bright.  
Lo Pan’s Eye has no limbs, but its mouth

brute force, driving intruders away or  
killing them outright. It drifts constantly,  
repositioning to keep everything in sight.  
No one knows who Lo Pan was. What  
matters is that places watched by the Eye  
rarely stay occupied.

Whobeast  
The Whobeast is a massive brute with a  
hulking body and an owl’s pale,  
unblinking face. It is violently territorial,  
charging anything that enters its ground  
with crushing force. Once it starts  
moving, it barrels through bodies without  
slowing, turning panic into wreckage in  
seconds.  
Terrorbirb  
The Terrorbirb is a towering, ﬂightless  
hunter built for open ground. It launches  
forward in brutal bursts of speed, closing  
distance before prey can scatter. The  
beak is thick and crushing, meant to end  
a ﬁght in a single strike as it barrels  
through whatever breaks ﬁrst. It doesn’t  
stop when something falls. It keeps  
moving, trampling bodies and panic alike,  
until the ﬁeld is empty or nothing left can  
run.  
WTEF  
WTEFs resemble Walters at a glance,  
sharing the same frog-like bodies and  
unsettling intelligence, but the similarities  
end quickly. They are far larger, more  
deliberate, and far more dangerous,  
massive creatures whose presence  
dominates whatever space they enter.  
Their exposed brains are fully enclosed  
beneath a naturally grown, clear dome.  
Tunnel Witch  
Tunnel Witches are Lurkers that learned  
to wait longer and think harder. They still  
hunt from tight, buried places, but now  
the tunnels bend around them in subtle,  
wrong ways. Sounds travel where they  
shouldn’t, shadows linger too long, and  
stone seems to shift just enough to make  
people doubt their footing. A Tunnel Witch  
doesn’t rush a kill. It lets fear do the work  
ﬁrst, watching intruders unravel before  
deciding who to take and who to let run.  
Unlike Walters, WTEFs wield magic with  
disturbing instinct. They test reactions,  
withdraw brieﬂy, and return once patterns  
are learned. They tolerate damage that  
would cripple lesser threats and press  
advantages with conﬁdence.  
If you encounter one, assume others are  
nearby and that the obvious killing blow  
will not work. Distance is the only reliable  
advantage.  
On the Limits of Prose in Describing Living Threats  
What is written here is the account of what these creatures are and how they are  
encountered. Prose is sufﬁcient for recognition, behavior, and warning, but it fails when  
exact limits matter. The full measures—how much punishment a creature can endure,  
how hard it strikes, how fast it moves, and where it fails—are recorded in an addendum  
to the Chronicle, where precision can be maintained without rewriting the account itself.

The Book of Feats  
People like to believe survival comes down to strength, luck, or preparedness.  
Those things matter, but they are not what separates the living from the dead over time.  
What matters is what a person learns to do when the world stops being fair, and how far  
they are willing to push themselves once learning is no longer enough.  
I have seen people do things that should not have been possible for them, not once, but  
repeatedly. Not miracles. Not magic. Something harder to explain. A way of moving,  
ﬁghting, enduring, or thinking that only appears after years of pressure. The kind of skill  
that does not fade when weapons break or plans fail.  
These are not tricks you pick up in a week. They are habits carved into the body and  
mind by repetition, injury, and survival. Some come from training, others from necessity,  
and a few from experiences no one should have lived through at all. Once learned, they  
do not leave easily.  
Feats are not evenly distributed. Two people can walk the same roads, ﬁght the same  
enemies, and still come away changed in different ways. One learns to strike faster.  
Another learns to endure pain longer. Another learns when not to ﬁght at all. None of  
these paths are safe, and none of them are guaranteed.  
What follows is not a guide on how to become exceptional. It is a record of what  
exceptional survivors have already become. If you recognize yourself in any of these,  
you did not learn it from a book. You earned it the hard way.  
On the Ways People Change  
For a long time I thought surviving meant becoming better at everything. Stronger,  
faster, harder to kill. That turned out not to be true. People do not improve evenly. They  
narrow. What they repeat, they sharpen. What they rely on, they reﬁne. Over time, those  
habits harden into something recognizable.  
Some people grow deeper into the roles they already know. Fighters ﬁght better. Priests  
become more certain in how they call on what answers them. Thieves learn to solve  
problems the way they always have. These changes are not about raw talent, but  
familiarity. The world keeps asking them the same kind of question, and eventually they  
stop hesitating before they answer.  
Others change through conﬂict itself. Repeated violence teaches its own lessons. These  
people learn how to move under pressure, how to strike without wasting effort, and how  
to stay upright when pain should have ended the ﬁght. You can tell them by how little  
they react when things turn ugly. They have been there too many times for it to feel new.  
After the Fall, The Chronicle of the Second Age, and its contents are ©2026 D. Ryan Mowry, All Rights Reserved.  
After the Fall The Chronicle of the Second Age  
Page 13 of 41  
There are also those who become broadly harder to kill without becoming especially  
dangerous. They endure. They resist fatigue, fear, and hardship longer than most. They  
learn small efﬁciencies that apply everywhere, regardless of weapon, terrain, or  
opponent. These are not specialists. They are survivors in the plainest sense of the  
word.  
A smaller group changes through forces that are not physical at all. Faith, study, or  
exposure to things left behind by the Fall alters how they prepare and how carefully they  
act. Their improvements come from restraint and structure rather than instinct. Even  
when their power looks controlled, it never feels casual, and it never comes without a  
cost.  
Then there are those who improve by avoiding confrontation altogether. They learn  
where attention gathers and how to step around it. They move differently, choose their  
moments carefully, and survive by not being present when strength alone would have  
failed. These people are rarely noticed until they are already gone.  
None of these changes happen by accident. They are responses to repeated pressure,  
shaped by what a person does most often and what they cannot afford to fail at. What  
follows are records of those patterns, written down so they can be recognized for what  
they are.  
On the Limits of Prose in Cataloguing Survival  
What is written here records the lessons people have learned to survive longer  
than they should have. Names and descriptions preserve meaning, but they cannot  
hold exact execution. The speciﬁc mechanics of these techniques are kept in an  
addendum to the Chronicle, where reﬁnement is possible without altering the story of  
how those lessons were earned.

The Book of Magic  
Magic is real. Before the fall, it was dismissed as illusion and trickery, or if it was real, it  
stayed hidden well enough that it did not matter. After the ﬁre, it did not stay hidden. It  
appears now without ceremony, without permission, and without regard for who is  
watching or what it costs them to see it. I have seen wounds close that should have  
killed a man, ﬁres burn where there was nothing to feed them, and words spoken once  
that left a place wrong long after the speaker was gone.  
Some say magic comes from the gods, and others claim the gods followed it into the  
world like scavengers drawn by blood. I have never seen enough to know which of them  
is lying. What I know is that when magic is used, something listens, and whatever it is  
does not think the way we do. People who pretend otherwise do not last long.  
Those who serve gods call their magic down and let it pass through them. They pray,  
they mark themselves, and they accept that what answers is not theirs to command.  
Sometimes it heals, sometimes it destroys, and sometimes it simply watches. I have  
seen Priests lose favor without warning, and others changed by power they did not ask  
for and could not refuse.  
There are others who carry magic in their blood, whether by birth, exposure, or  
inheritance from things that should not have survived the Fall. Their power comes  
quickly and violently, without ritual or preparation, and it frightens people because it  
cannot be reasoned with. Settlements tolerate them only when they must, and even  
then they are watched like unexploded ordnance.  
The most dangerous, in my experience, are the ones who study it. They write spells  
down, copy symbols, and convince themselves that repetition equals control. They  
remind me of the engineers of the old world, certain that understanding a system meant  
they could not be harmed by it. Magic has outlived every one of those assumptions.  
Magic does not rebuild what was lost. It grows in the cracks left behind. It works reliably,  
and that is what makes it dangerous, because it tempts people into thinking reliability is  
the same as safety. I am writing this so the next person understands what I did too late:  
if you see magic used easily, leave. If you see it used carefully, keep your distance. And  
if you feel it answer when you did not call, do not stay to ﬁnd out why.  
Magic, and those who use it  
Magic does not belong to a single kind of person. It appears in different hands for  
different reasons, and it behaves differently depending on who is holding it. Some  
people approach it carefully, others instinctively, and some only through faith. The  
results can look similar from a distance, but they do not come from the same place, and  
they do not fail in the same way.  
After the Fall, The Chronicle of the Second Age, and its contents are ©2026 D. Ryan Mowry, All Rights Reserved.  
After the Fall The Chronicle of the Second Age  
Page 15 of 41  
There are those who treat magic as a thing to be learned, broken down, and repeated.  
They record what works and avoid what does not, building patterns from what survives.  
Others never learn it at all, but carry it inside themselves, reacting to danger before  
thought has time to intervene. And there are those who never claim it as theirs, who  
speak names and symbols and allow power to pass through them without ever  
pretending to own it. I have seen all three, sometimes working together, sometimes  
tearing each other apart.  
Not all magic demands the same effort. Some effects come quickly, as if the world is  
already leaning in that direction and only needs a push. Other workings resist being  
shaped, requiring preparation, focus, and visible commitment before they answer. The  
difference is obvious even to someone watching from a safe distance. One kind  
happens in the moment. The other announces itself, and gives you time to regret being  
nearby.  
People who survive around magic learn to recognize these differences without knowing  
why they exist. They learn when to move, when to hide, and when to hope the person  
casting knows what they are doing. Magic may be reliable, but the people using it are  
not, and the world remembers the difference.  
Warlocks  
Warlocks do not study magic. They live it. Their power is innate, carried in blood,  
mutation, inheritance, or exposure to forces that did not disappear with the old world.  
Warlocks cast spells the way others breathe or bleed, without ritual, preparation, or  
permission. Magic comes to them quickly and violently, often before they understand  
what it costs.  
This makes Warlocks dangerous, but also honest. They do not pretend magic is safe or  
orderly. They know it works because it answers them every time, and because it never  
lets them forget it is there. Many Warlocks display physical signs of this connection,  
though not always in ways that are immediately obvious.  
Settlements tolerate Warlocks cautiously. Their power is useful in emergencies and  
terrifying in close quarters. A Warlock who loses control can do as much damage as a  
weapon malfunction or a structural collapse, and there is rarely warning before it  
happens.  
Some Warlocks learn restraint through experience. Others burn out, are hunted, or  
disappear into places where no one can tell the difference. Unlike Wizards or Priests,  
Warlocks do not ask where their power comes from. They are too busy surviving its  
presence.

After the Fall The Chronicle of the Second Age

Wizards  
Wizards are those who have come to learn that magic can be understood. They do  
not pray for power, and they are not born carrying it. Wizards learn magic the way the  
old world learned everything else: through study, repetition, and the belief that systems  
can be mastered if one works hard enough. They write spells down, catalog symbols,  
and pass knowledge between one another as if it were a craft rather than a risk.  
This approach works, most of the time. Wizards are capable of precise, deliberate  
magic, often more controlled than that of other spellcasters. Their spells are repeatable,  
structured, and predictable in a way that makes them valuable to settlements and  
organizations that rely on planning rather than faith or instinct.  
That belief in understanding is also their greatest weakness. Wizards often mistake  
familiarity for safety, and documentation for ownership. They assume that because a  
spell has been written, copied, and cast before, it will behave the same way again.  
Magic does not always agree.  
Wizards tend to gather in places where knowledge can be protected: towers, ruins,  
sealed facilities, or buried vaults of pre-Fall data. They are more likely than other  
spellcasters to survive long enough to leave records, and more likely to leave behind  
places no one should enter afterward.  
When a Wizard fails, it is rarely sudden. It is cumulative, built from small assumptions  
stacked too high. Their mistakes linger, embedded in spellbooks, altered environments,  
and apprentices who inherit more than they understand.  
Priests  
To be a Priest in After the Fall is to serve as a conduit for a power that is undeniably  
real and fundamentally external. Gods exist. Their nature is debated, their motives  
unclear, and their truths fragmented, but their inﬂuence is undeniable. Priests are those  
rare individuals through whom divine power is actively channeled. This power does not  
originate within the Priest. It is granted, invoked, and mediated through devotion,  
symbolism, and belief.  
Priests do not command magic in the way other magic users do. They ask for it. They  
invoke it. They allow it to act through them. Their spells are expressions of divine will  
ﬁltered through mortal intent, shaped by the nature of the god they serve rather than  
personal mastery or study.  
This relationship is not without consequence. Priests are often marked by physical  
manifestations reﬂecting their deity’s inﬂuence. These signs are cosmetic, but  
meaningful, and are frequently recognized by other followers of the same god. Over  
After the Fall, The Chronicle of the Second Age, and its contents are ©2026 D. Ryan Mowry, All Rights Reserved.  
After the Fall The Chronicle of the Second Age  
Page 17 of 41  
time, devotion shapes identity, perspective, and presence, even when a Priest does not  
consciously seek change.  
In After the Fall, the gods themselves are distant, fractured, and not bound by mortal  
morality. Some are newly risen powers shaped by the aftermath of the world’s  
destruction. Others are ancient beings whose inﬂuence predates humanity itself. Priests  
do not command these entities, nor do they fully understand them. They serve them  
willingly, dutifully, or out of necessity and act as vessels through which divine will,  
philosophy, or entropy manifests in the world.  
Not all priests are holy in the traditional sense. Some serve gods of justice, unity, or  
preservation. Others draw power from indifferent forces of knowledge, war, or survival.  
Still others bind themselves to primordial entities whose motives lie beyond morality,  
sanity, or human understanding. What unites all priests is not goodness, but connection.  
Importantly, worship alone does not make one a Priest. Any character may honor a god,  
carry symbols, or pray for favor. Only Priests receive divine magic. A Wizard who  
worships a god still draws power from study. A Hunter who prays before battle still relies  
on skill. Priesthood is not belief, but connection.  
Priestly magic uses the same core mechanics as all other characters. There are no  
special subsystems unique to divine power. Prayers, miracles, and divine spells are  
resolved using standard rolls, resources, and conditions already deﬁned in the core  
rules and class descriptions. Any limitations, expectations, or consequences of priestly  
power arise from the nature of the deity served, not from unique mechanical exceptions.  
A priest’s relationship with their deity is central to their identity. While the Priest class  
deﬁnes what a character can do, the deity deﬁnes why they do it, what is asked of them,  
and what that power ultimately costs.  
On the Known Gods  
The gods did not disappear when the world burned. If anything, they became  
easier to notice. Whether they existed before the Fall or emerged from what was left  
behind is still argued by people with the luxury to argue. Out here, the distinction does  
not matter. The known gods answer. Sometimes clearly, sometimes indirectly,  
sometimes in ways that only make sense after something is lost.  
They are not uniﬁed. They do not agree with one another. They do not share values,  
morality, or even perspective. Some demand devotion, others tolerate it, and some do  
not appear to care whether they are worshipped at all. What they have in common is  
inﬂuence. Where they are acknowledged, the world bends slightly out of shape.  
Priests speak of the known gods as patrons, judges, forces, or principles. Ordinary  
people tend to describe them more simply, as things that notice you if you are careless.  
Shrines rise and fall, names change, symbols fracture, but the presence remains. A god  
ignored is not always a god gone.

Not all of the known gods are concerned with humanity. Some predate it. Others treat  
mortals as tools, tests, or background noise. A few seem almost invested, though never  
in ways that are entirely safe. Faith does not guarantee protection, and disbelief does  
not guarantee distance.  
What follows are the known gods most commonly named, feared, or survived in the  
Second Age. This is not a complete list. It is only the names that still answer often  
enough to matter.  
Abaddon  
Alignment: Evil Alternate Names: King of  
the Pit, The Destroyer, Angel of the Abyss

the annihilation that follows inevitable  
collapse.  
Abaddon is a god associated with endings  
that cannot be averted. Unlike deities of war  
who revel in conﬂict or conquest, Abaddon  
embodies what comes after: cities reduced to  
rubble, civilizations broken beyond recovery,  
and lives extinguished not through struggle,  
but through overwhelming ﬁnality.  
Image BoM:1 The Sigil of Abaddon  
In many traditions, Abaddon is not a creator of  
chaos, but its executor. Destruction under  
Abaddon’s inﬂuence is portrayed as purposeful and absolute, stripping away what has  
already failed or grown corrupt. Followers often view Abaddon not as cruel, but as  
necessary: a force that clears away what must end so that something else may  
eventually arise, even if Abaddon itself does not care what follows.  
Interpretations of Abaddon vary widely. Some worshippers see him as a divine judge  
who punishes decadence and decay, while others revere him purely as an agent of  
annihilation, valuing destruction for its own sake. In all cases, Abaddon is feared rather  
than loved, respected rather than trusted.

Unlike creator gods who shape the world through intention, Abraxis embodies cause  
without purpose. It is the principle that something happened, not because it was meant  
to, but because it could. Followers of Abraxis do not pray for intervention. They seek  
understanding of the hidden mechanisms that govern reality, believing that meaning is a  
consequence of causality rather than design.  
Devotion to Abraxis is most commonly found among cultic mystics, secretive orders,  
and esoteric scholars who believe that truth lies beneath appearances. Rituals focus on  
revelation, paradox, and the contemplation of origins rather than morality or outcome.  
Abraxis does not reward faith, punish disbelief, or clarify its intent. It simply exists, and  
by existing, allows everything else to follow.  
Interpretations of Abraxis vary. Some consider it the silent foundation upon which all  
other gods act. Others believe it to be indifferent even to divinity itself, a god that began  
the process and then withdrew from consequence.

truth, even as their beliefs become increasingly detached from reality.  
Baphomet’s inﬂuence spreads through organized deception, secret hierarchies, and  
teachings designed to entrap rather than enlighten. Doctrine is layered, contradictory,  
and deliberately obscured, ensuring that devotion deepens even as comprehension  
diminishes.  
Interpretations of Baphomet vary among worshippers. Some see him as a revealer of  
hidden truths denied by other gods, while others embrace him as a destroyer of false  
morality. In every case, devotion to Baphomet reshapes belief into a tool of control.

clearly in moments of courage, sacriﬁce, or impending death.  
The Bloom  
Alignment: Any Alternate Names: Mother  
Nature, The Mother, The Worldroot  
Description: A god of nature, renewal, and  
the inevitable persistence of life.  
The Bloom is a god associated with nature in  
all its forms, growth, renewal, and the  
certainty that life endures. Unlike gods tied to  
civilization, morality, or singular events, The  
Bloom represents the living world as it exists  
and continues, indifferent to human ambition,  
collapse, or belief.  
The Bloom has always existed. Long before  
Image BoM:5 The Sigil of The Bloom  
cities rose and long after they fell, life  
continued to grow, adapt, and reclaim the world.  
Over time, as civilization expanded and nature was  
pushed aside, The Bloom faded from common worship, not through weakness, but  
through neglect and forgetting.

After the Fall, as forests spread into ruins, fungi thrived in broken structures, and  
animals returned to abandoned places, The Bloom was rediscovered. As nature  
reasserts itself, devotion to The Bloom grows stronger. Followers believe this  
resurgence is not a reaction to destruction, but a reminder that nature never truly  
leaves, it only waits.  
Worship of The Bloom is practical rather than doctrinal. It is expressed through  
cultivation, stewardship, and acceptance of natural cycles. Farmers, healers,  
scavengers, mutants, and those who live close to the land often honor The Bloom  
without formal rites, simply by allowing life to grow where it will.  
Interpretations of The Bloom vary. Some see it as nurturing and restorative, others as  
vast and indifferent. Across all beliefs, The Bloom represents renewal, healing, and  
inevitability, the certainty that life continues regardless of intention or consequence.  
Appearance  
The Bloom is rarely depicted as a single, ﬁxed form. Common representations include:  
• A humanoid ﬁgure entwined with plant  
life, roots, or ﬂowering growth  
• A form that feels alive and changing,  
even when still  
• A presence marked by leaves, vines,  
moss, or fungi emerging naturally  
Some traditions depict The Bloom as gentle and maternal, while others portray it as  
immense and impersonal, reﬂecting the many ways nature is experienced.  
Priest Manifestations  
Accounts of priests devoted to The Bloom frequently describe physical traits reﬂecting  
living growth and natural vitality:  
• Plants in the surrounding area appear  
drawn to the priest, growing more lush,  
verdant, and alive in their presence,  
even in poor soil or harsh conditions  
• Hair that shows subtle signs of life, with  
leaves, moss, or lichen interwoven  
naturally among strands  
• Minor injuries that visibly close or knit  
quickly, leaving no scars and  
resembling natural regeneration rather  
than recovery  
• Plant matter or fungi may grow directly  
from the priest’s body, such as small  
branches, leaves, mushrooms, moss, or  
lichen emerging from the skin without  
pain or injury, usually subtle but  
sometimes dramatic and unmistakable

These manifestations vary widely. Some priests show only environmental signs, while

Div-e Sepid  
Alignment: Indifferent Alternate Names: The  
Northern Prince, Eridu, The White Demon  
Description: A god of sorcery, forbidden

Div-e Sepid is a god associated with magic  
claimed through intellect and domination, rather  
than wisdom or humility. He embodies the belief  
that knowledge is meant to be taken, not  
granted, and that the consequences of power  
are irrelevant compared to its acquisition. In this  
sense, Div-e Sepid stands as a cautionary  
ﬁgure, a living reminder of what occurs when  
Image BoM:6 The Sigil of Div-e Sepid  
mastery eclipses responsibility.  
In myth, Div-e Sepid is feared less for cruelty than for indifference. He does not seek to  
corrupt, uplift, or destroy. He simply pursues understanding and power, regardless of  
what must be broken, reshaped, or consumed in the process. His followers believe that  
magic is a force meant to be mastered absolutely, and that those unable to withstand its  
cost are unworthy of it.  
Devotion to Div-e Sepid is most common among spellcasters, occult scholars, and  
secretive orders who reject imposed limits on magical inquiry. Worship is often solitary  
or conducted in small circles, practiced in isolated towers, sealed chambers, or  
forgotten ruins where dangerous knowledge can be pursued without interference.  
Interpretations of Div-e Sepid vary. Some view him as a necessary warning embodied in  
divine form, others as proof that power alone deﬁnes truth. All agree that his inﬂuence  
reshapes those who follow him, whether they intend it or not.  
Appearance  
Div-e Sepid is most often described as a towering, pale ﬁgure, marked by unnatural  
proportions. Common depictions include:  
• A massive white or bone-colored body  
• A neck and shoulders reminiscent of a  
great beast rather than a man  
• An upper form branching like dead or  
frost-covered trees

Hastur  
Alignment: Any (Primordial) Alternate  
Names: The King in Yellow  
Description: A Primordial god of forbidden

Hastur is a Primordial entity whose inﬂuence  
manifests not through conquest or destruction,  
but through ideas that rot the mind.  
Knowledge of Hastur spreads like a contagion  
through forbidden texts, recurring symbols,  
unﬁnished plays, whispered phrases, and art  
that feels wrong in ways that are difﬁcult to  
articulate.  
Image BoM:8 The Sigil of Hastur  
Those touched by Hastur often insist they are not mad. They claim instead to see truths  
others refuse to acknowledge, or patterns hidden beneath the world’s surface. Exposure  
to Hastur’s inﬂuence blurs the line between revelation and delusion, certainty and  
obsession.  
Unlike gods who demand worship, Hastur often appears to allow itself to be discovered.  
Devotion may begin accidentally by reading the wrong passage, performing the wrong  
scene, or gazing too long upon a symbol that should not exist. By the time a follower  
realizes what they have found, it is often too late to turn away.  
Interpretations of Hastur vary wildly. Some believe it is a god of ultimate truth, others a  
parasite that feeds on meaning itself. All agree that once Hastur’s presence is felt, it  
cannot be fully forgotten.  
Appearance  
Hastur is most commonly depicted indirectly rather than seen directly. Descriptions often  
include:  
• A tattered yellow robe or shroud,  
obscuring what lies beneath  
• A presence that feels observed, even  
when no form is visible  
• A sense of impossible angles or  
proportions when glimpsed  
Many accounts emphasize that Hastur’s true form is either unknowable or actively  
concealed, and that attempts to depict it directly often end in madness or contradiction.

Laverna is a god associated with crime as

Unlike gods who condemn theft as moral

In traditions devoted to Laverna, theft is not mindless greed but strategy. She is revered

the truth that systems of power often leave no honest path to survival.  
Devotion to Laverna is informal and pragmatic. Shrines are hidden, offerings are subtle,  
and prayers are whispered rather than proclaimed. Laverna does not demand loyalty so  
much as discretion. She rewards cleverness, planning, and the ability to disappear  
when necessary.  
Interpretations of Laverna vary widely. Some worshippers see her as a protector of the  
downtrodden, while others embrace her as a patron of crime for its own sake. In both  
cases, Laverna embodies the thin line between justice and exploitation, and the ease  
with which one becomes the other.

Devotion to Lillith is often solitary or practiced in small, loosely connected circles. Her

Interpretations of Lillith vary widely. Some revere her as a liberator and teacher, others

Devotion to Utu is often public and communal. He is honored in courts, assemblies, and  
places where oaths are sworn and disputes settled. His worship emphasizes honesty,  
lawful conduct, and accountability, even when transparency carries personal cost.  
Interpretations of Utu vary. Some see him as just and righteous, others as merciless

light will reach all things.

Worship of Y’golonac is never passive. Its followers believe that meaning is found  
through the breaking of limits and that morality itself is an artiﬁcial barrier imposed to  
deny truth. Devotion often manifests through secret rites, forbidden practices, or  
deliberate acts of desecration intended to draw the god’s attention.  
Interpretations of Y’golonac differ among its followers. Some see it as a god of liberation  
through excess, others as a force that strips away false identity until only base desire  
remains. All agree that service to Y’golonac leaves nothing untouched and nothing  
unchanged.

Appearance  
Y’golonac is rarely depicted as a whole form. Instead, accounts describe partial  
manifestations, including:  
• A mouth appearing in unnatural places,  
such as the palms of hands or the soles  
• Flesh that seems capable of opening,  
folding, or speaking where it should not  
of feet  
ꢀ
• A presence that feels intrusive and  
intimate rather than distant  
Descriptions emphasize that Y’golonac’s form is inseparable from violation itself and  
that to perceive it fully is to invite it closer.  
Priest Manifestations  
Accounts of priests devoted to Y’golonac frequently describe disturbing but subtle  
physical alterations, inspired by mythos depictions:  
• Additional mouths forming along the  
body, most commonly in the palms or  
inner forearms  
• Tongues that appear too long or too  
ﬂexible, moving in unsettling ways when  
exposed  
• Lips or teeth visible beneath the skin,  
as if something inside is trying to speak  
• Skin that dimples or puckers when  
touched, resembling suppressed  
speech or breath  
These manifestations are not uniform. Some priests display only a single sign, while  
others exhibit several. In many cases, these features remain concealed beneath  
clothing until revealed intentionally.  
Zvilpogghua  
Alignment: Any (Primordial) Alternate  
Names: The Feaster from the Stars  
Description: A Primordial god of endless  
hunger, cosmic consumption, and the erasure  
of meaning through appetite.  
Zvilpogghua is a Primordial entity deﬁned by  
consumption without satisfaction. It is  
associated with hunger that cannot be ﬁlled,  
appetites that grow rather than diminish, and  
the slow realization that nothing consumed is  
ever enough. Unlike gods of gluttony or  
excess, Zvilpogghua does not revel in

Its inﬂuence is often felt in places where resources vanish inexplicably, where  
settlements starve despite abundance, or where predators consume far more than  
survival demands. Followers of Zvilpogghua interpret hunger as a cosmic truth: the  
universe itself devours, and to feed is to align with its fundamental nature.  
Interpretations of Zvilpogghua differ. Some see it as the inevitable end of all things,  
others as a god of survival taken to its most brutal extreme. All accounts agree that  
devotion to Zvilpogghua replaces desire with need, and need with an ever-widening  
void.  
Appearance  
Zvilpogghua is most often described as a vast, bloated form, drifting or pressing against  
reality rather than standing within it. Accounts vary, but commonly include:  
• A body swollen beyond natural  
proportion  
• A sense that its shape is deﬁned by  
what it has consumed rather than any  
original form  
• Distended, sagging ﬂesh or mass that  
appears heavy and overﬁlled  
Witnesses frequently describe the impression that Zvilpogghua is always feeding, even  
when no mouth or method of consumption is visible.  
Priest Manifestations

On the Limits of Prose in Recording Magic  
These pages describe magic as it is understood and invoked. Words can explain  
intent and consequence, but they are unreliable when precision decides survival. The  
exact workings of spells—their costs, ranges, durations, and limits—are kept in an  
addendum to the Chronicle, where errors can be corrected without pretending they  
never occurred.

Parting Notes  
I did not write this to explain the Second Age of the Deadlands. The world does not  
feel the need to explain itself, and anyone who claims to understand it fully is lying. I  
wrote this to leave marks behind to help those who come after me, the way others left  
roads, warnings, and names scratched into walls that were already falling apart.  
Everything recorded here was learned the hard way. None of it is complete. None of it is  
safe to rely on. It reﬂects what survived long enough to be noticed, not what deserved  
to. There are gaps where people died too quickly, and silences where no one came  
back to tell the rest of us what happened.  
Use what you recognize. Ignore what you do not. Add your own notes if you live long  
enough to earn them.  
If these words matter to you, then they were worth writing.
